summary: Defines the Host-bit (H-bit) for OSPFv2, which lets a router advertise that it is a non-transit router so other routers will not send transit traffic through it. It also describes the changes needed to support the bit and updates RFC 6987.

plainLanguage.summary: This document adds one bit to the OSPFv2 router advertisement. A router that sets it says that it should receive traffic for its own addresses but should not carry traffic between other routers.

questions: how can an ospf router avoid transit traffic
how does ospf avoid transit traffic
what is ospf host router capability
how does ospf graceful isolation work
subtitle: A single bit that lets an OSPFv2 router say: send traffic to me, never through me.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 has no way for a router to push transit traffic away when it sits on the only or shortest path, so raising a metric only helps when another path exists.
tldr.mechanism: A new bit in the router-LSA, the H-bit, marks a router as a host router. Routers that support it exclude it from the transit part of the shortest path calculation.
tldr.outcome: A router can be isolated for maintenance or overwhelmed capacity without blackholing traffic. RFC 8770 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 10041.

today: RFC 8770 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2020. It updates RFC 6987, and it was later updated by RFC 10041. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Router Might Want to Repel Traffic
sections.content:
OSPFv2 specifies a shortest path first algorithm that identifies transit vertices from their adjacencies. It therefore has no mechanism to prevent traffic transiting a participating node when that node is a transit vertex in the only existing or shortest path to the destination. Using metrics to make the node undesirable helps to repel traffic only if an alternative better route exists.

A mechanism to move traffic away from the shortest path is useful in several cases.

  • Graceful isolation of a router. To avoid blackhole scenarios when there is a reload and possibly long reconvergence times.
  • Closet switches. Switches that are not usually used for transit traffic but need to take part in the topology.
  • Overloaded routers. A router that could use such a capability to repel traffic temporarily until it stabilises.
  • BGP route reflectors. Known as virtual route reflectors, these are not in the forwarding path but sit in central locations such as data centres. They are used for route distribution and cannot forward transit traffic, yet they need to learn the OSPF topology to perform the shortest path computation for optimal routes and reachability resolution for their clients.

The document describes the functionality provided by the Host-bit, the H-bit. It prevents other OSPFv2 routers from using the host router by excluding it in path calculations for transit traffic in the OSPFv2 routing domain. When the H-bit is set, the calculation of the shortest path tree for an area is modified to include a check that transit vertices do not have the H-bit set. To repel traffic effectively the document also updates RFC 6987, so that Type 2 External and Not-So-Stubby Area link state advertisements are advertised with a high cost. OSPFv3 defines an option bit, the R-bit, for router LSAs, and the H-bit supports similar functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a router should be reachable but should not be a stepping stone for other traffic: a route reflector that sits in the middle of the network but cannot forward, or a router being reloaded. Raising its metric only deters traffic when another route exists, which is why a separate flag is needed.

sections.title: The Host Bit
sections.content:
The document defines a new router-LSA bit, the Host-bit or H-bit. An OSPFv2 router advertising a router-LSA with the H-bit set indicates that it MUST NOT be used as a transit router by the other OSPFv2 routers in the area that support the H-bit functionality. If the H-bit is not set, backward compatibility is achieved, because the behaviour is the same as in RFC 2328.

Bit H is the high-order bit of the OSPF flags, the first of the eight option bits, followed by two reserved bits and the E, B, V, W and N bits.

When the H-bit is set, the OSPFv2 router is a host, that is non-transit, router and is incapable of forwarding transit traffic. In this mode the other OSPFv2 routers in the area MUST NOT use the host router for transit traffic but may send traffic to its local destinations.

An OSPFv2 router originating a router-LSA with the H-bit set MUST advertise all its non-stub links with a link cost of MaxLinkMetric, as in RFC 6987.

When the H-bit is set, an Area Border Router MUST advertise the same H-bit setting in its self-originated router-LSAs for all attached areas. The consistency of the setting prevents inter-area traffic transiting through the router, by suppressing advertisements of prefixes from other routers in the area in its summary-LSAs. Only IPv4 prefixes associated with its local interfaces MUST be advertised in summary-LSAs, to give reachability to end hosts attached to a router with the H-bit set.

When the H-bit is set, the host router cannot act as an Autonomous System Border Router, since ASBRs are transit routers for prefixes typically imported through redistribution from other routing protocols. Non-local IPv4 prefixes, for example those imported from other routing protocols, SHOULD NOT be advertised in AS-external LSAs if the H-bit is set. Some use cases, such as an overloaded router or a router being gracefully isolated, may benefit from continued advertisements of non-local prefixes, and in those cases the Type 2 metric in AS-external LSAs MUST be set to LSInfinity to repel traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The bit goes in the router advertisement itself. A router that sets it also has to raise the cost of all its real links to the maximum, so that routers which do not understand the bit still avoid sending traffic through it.

sections.title: How the Shortest Path Calculation Changes
sections.content:
The shortest path calculation of Section 16.1 of RFC 2328 is modified so that routers originating router-LSAs with the H-bit set are not used for transit traffic. Step (2) is modified to include a check on the H-bit, and the other sub-procedures of that step are unchanged.

In the modified step, the router takes the vertex just added to the tree, calls it vertex V, and examines the LSA associated with it, which is a lookup in area A's link state database. If this is a router-LSA and the H-bit of the router-LSA is set and vertex V is not the root, then the router should not be used for transit and step (3) is executed immediately. If the LSA is a router-LSA and its V bit is set, area A's TransitCapability is set to TRUE. In any case each link described by the LSA gives the cost to an adjacent vertex, and the links are handled as before.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is in the algorithm that builds the map of routes. When a router is added to that map as an intermediate hop, its advertisement is checked: if the bit is set, the router is not used as a stepping stone.

sections.title: Autodiscovery and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
To reduce the possibility of routing loops from a partial deployment, the document defines an OSPF Router Information LSA capability bit as in RFC 7770. The RI LSA MUST be area-scoped. Autodiscovery through the announcement of the OSPF Host Router capability ensures that the H-bit functionality and its associated shortest path changes MUST only take effect if all the routers in a given OSPF area support it.

In normal operation the RI LSA may fail to reach all the routers in an area in a timely manner. For example, if a new router without H-bit support joins an area that previously had only H-bit-capable routers with the bit set, it may take some time for the RI LSA to propagate to all of them. While it is propagating, the routers in the area gradually detect the presence of a router that does not support the capability and revert to the normal shortest path calculation. During the propagation time the area as a whole is unsure of the status of the new router, and this situation can cause temporary transient loops.

Three recommendations mitigate those transient loops. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to provide a configuration parameter to manually override enforcement of the H-bit functionality in partial deployments where the topology guarantees that the routers which do not support the bit do not compute routes resulting in routing loops. All routers with the H-bit set MUST advertise all of their non-stub links with a metric equal to MaxLinkMetric in their LSAs, to prevent OSPFv2 routers, unless there is a last-resort path, that do not support the bit from attempting to use the non-stub links for transit traffic. And all routers supporting the bit MUST check the RI LSAs of all the nodes in the area to verify that all nodes support it before actively using the feature; if any router does not advertise the OSPF Host Router capability, the shortest path modifications MUST NOT be used in the area.
sections.plainLanguage: If only some routers understand the new bit, the network could loop. So the routers first agree, through a capability advertisement, that everyone understands it, and only then act on it. While that agreement is spreading, the old behaviour is used.

sections.title: External Routes and Type 2 Metrics
sections.content:
When calculating the path to a prefix in an OSPF AS-external LSA or NSSA LSA with a Type 2 metric, the advertised Type 2 metric is taken as more significant than the OSPF intra-area or inter-area path. Advertising the links with MaxLinkMetric, as RFC 6987 does, therefore does not discourage transit traffic when calculating AS-external or NSSA routes with Type 2 metrics.

The document consequently updates RFC 6987 so that the Type 2 metric in any self-originated AS-external LSAs or NSSA LSAs is advertised as LSInfinity-1. If the H-bit is set, the Type 2 metric MUST be set to LSInfinity.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic coming from outside the OSPF area is judged by a different rule, and it would ignore the raised link cost. So the external advertisements get their own very high cost to push that traffic away as well.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has registered the value 0x80 for the Host, H-bit, in the OSPFv2 Router Properties Registry. It has also registered bit number 7 for the OSPF Host Router capability in the OSPF Router Informational Capability Bits registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the registry for the value that carries the bit and for the capability bit that advertises support for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces the H-bit, a capability feature that restricts the use of a router for transit while only its local destinations remain reachable. This is a subset of the operations of a normal router, so it should not introduce security considerations beyond those already known in OSPFv2. The feature does introduce the advertisement of host router capability information to all the OSPFv2 routers in an area, which can be used to discover and verify that all the routers in the area support the capability before the feature is turned on.

In the event that a rogue or buggy router advertises its capability incorrectly, there are three scenarios. If the router does not have the capability but sends the H-bit set in its LSAs, a routing loop is possible, but this is mitigated by the fact that the router should be avoided anyway and by its MaxLinkMetric link costs; a router advertising the H-bit capability without its link metric cost equal to MaxLinkMetric could be a rogue router and should be avoided. If the router has the capability but sends the H-bit clear, it merely prevents the other H-bit routers in the area from running the modified shortest path calculation, and the impacts are mitigated because those other routers also advertise the MaxLinkMetric cost and so are still avoided unless they are the last-resort path. If a rogue router is on the only transit path for some destinations and sends the H-bit set for no valid reason, it effectively partitions the network, but this case is indistinguishable from an operator consciously setting the bit to perform maintenance on a router that is on the only transit path, and OSPF continues to function within the partitioned domains.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that lies about this capability could cause loops or split the network. The safeguards are the maximum link cost it must also advertise, and the fact that a partitioned network still works inside each part.

items.title: Graceful isolation
items.text: Taking a router out of service without blackholing traffic, during a reload with long reconvergence times.

items.title: Closet switches
items.text: Switches that are not usually used to carry transit traffic but still need to take part in the topology.

items.text: A router repels traffic temporarily until it has stabilised.

items.title: BGP route reflectors
items.text: Virtual route reflectors that distribute routes but cannot forward transit traffic, and still need the OSPF topology.

viz.caption: THE BIT SET AGAINST THE BIT CLEAR (RFC 8770, SECTION 3)

left.title: H-bit set
left.desc: The router is a host router. Other routers must not use it for transit traffic, but may send traffic to its local destinations.

right.title: H-bit clear
right.desc: Behaviour is the same as in RFC 2328, so routers that do not understand the feature are unaffected.

viz.caption: THE THREE SAFEGUARDS AGAINST TRANSIENT LOOPS (RFC 8770, SECTION 5)

items.title: A manual override
items.text: A configuration parameter lets an operator enforce the feature in a partial deployment where the topology is known to be safe.

items.title: Maximum link cost
items.text: A router with the bit set must advertise all its non-stub links with a cost of MaxLinkMetric, so routers that do not understand the bit still avoid it.

items.title: Check every router first
items.text: Routers supporting the bit must confirm that every node in the area advertises the capability before using the feature at all.

viz.caption: THE VALUES THIS DOCUMENT FIXES (RFC 8770, SECTIONS 3, 6 AND 7)

items.label: Host, H-bit
items.desc: The value in the OSPFv2 Router Properties Registry that carries the bit in the router-LSA.

items.label: OSPF Host Router
items.desc: The bit number in the OSPF Router Informational Capability Bits registry.

items.label: Non-stub link cost
items.desc: The cost a router with the bit set must advertise for all of its non-stub links.

items.label: Type 2 metric
items.desc: The value the update to RFC 6987 sets for self-originated AS-external and NSSA LSAs.

items.label: Type 2 metric with the bit
items.desc: The value the Type 2 metric MUST take when the H-bit is set.
